name: Ketogenic diet face

lead: People use a ketogenic diet to get a leaner, less puffy face: slimmer cheeks, a sharper jaw and less bloat. The face gets leaner as overall body fat comes down and water retention drops.

Cutting carbohydrate makes the liver produce ketone bodies for fuel, and low-carb diets can produce somewhat greater short-term weight loss than low-fat diets. A 2022 Cochrane review found no weight-loss advantage over balanced diets at two years. The diet was developed in the 1920s for epilepsy, and no study has measured facial appearance on it.

paras: People follow it as a long-running eating pattern: high fat, moderate protein, very few carbohydrates, usually tracked with food logs or ketone strips. It is often combined with lifting or cardio and with a calorie deficit. Many users report noticing less bloat within the first couple of weeks, with fat-loss changes in the face taking longer as body fat drops.

Reported effects include constipation, raised cholesterol, nutrient gaps and, rarely, ketoacidosis. It is contraindicated in certain metabolic disorders. People with diabetes on medication, kidney or liver disease, or who are pregnant are generally advised to get medical input before starting.

chain: Fat loss and less water retention
angle.text: Appearance communities use a ketogenic diet to lean out the cheeks and reduce puffiness: very low carbohydrate intake leads to fat loss and lower water retention, which shows in the face. Weight-loss studies exist for the diet, and facial appearance specifically has not been measured.

lead: The ketogenic diet face refers to the belief in appearance communities that a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat ketogenic diet leans out the face, reducing puffiness and cheek fat. The diet itself restricts carbohydrate so that the liver produces ketone bodies as fuel, and was developed in the 1920s as a treatment for epilepsy.[1]

Low-carbohydrate diets can produce somewhat greater short-term weight loss than low-fat diets, but a 2022 Cochrane review cited in encyclopedic sources found no benefit over balanced diets at two years.[2] No published trial found in the sources reviewed has measured facial fat or facial appearance on a ketogenic diet.[1][2]

paras: The classic ketogenic diet is high in fat with adequate protein and little carbohydrate, commonly a 4:1 ratio of fat to protein plus carbohydrate. Russell Wilder at the Mayo Clinic coined the term in 1921, and in 1925 Mynie Peterman reported that 60 percent of 37 children became seizure-free.[1] Use declined after anticonvulsant drugs arrived and revived in the 1990s.[1]
Low-carbohydrate diets for weight control have a longer history, including William Banting's 1863 letter and Robert Atkins's 1972 book.[2]

Proponents in appearance communities say that carbohydrate restriction reduces water retention and inflammation so that facial bloat falls, and that body-fat loss reveals bone structure. These are community claims; the sources reviewed contain no studies of facial effects.

A 2017 Endocrine Society estimate cited in encyclopedic sources put the short-term advantage of low-carbohydrate over low-fat diets at about 100 kcal per day, fading over time.[2] The 2022 Cochrane review found no advantage at two years, and researchers attribute weight loss mainly to calorie restriction and adherence.[2] The carbohydrate-insulin hypothesis, which holds that insulin drives fat gain, was reported as not supported by a 2012 NuSI-funded study.[2]

Reported effects of ketogenic diets include constipation, low-grade acidosis and raised cholesterol, and in children slowed growth, fractures and kidney stones.[1] Low-carbohydrate diets are associated in reviews with headache, halitosis, muscle cramps and weakness, and rarely ketoacidosis.[2]

The American Heart Association found insufficient evidence for ketogenic diets to promote heart health, and the American College of Cardiology recommends clinician discussion before very low-carbohydrate diets.[2] The diet is contraindicated in disorders such as pyruvate carboxylase deficiency and porphyria.[1]

No studies found on facial fat or appearance. Trials of ketogenic diets have examined epilepsy, where a 2018 Cochrane review of 11 randomized trials found that about 38 percent of children on the diet in the largest trial had half or fewer seizures versus 6 percent of controls, and body-weight loss in adults.[1][2]

timeline.event: Russell Wilder coins the term ketogenic diet at the Mayo Clinic.[1]
William Banting publishes a letter on a low-carbohydrate weight-control diet.[2]
Robert Atkins publishes Dr. Atkins' Diet Revolution.[2]
Cochrane review finds no weight-loss advantage of low-carbohydrate diets at two years.[2]
